source.title: Safety Alignment Should be Made More than just A Few Attention Heads
source.authors: Chao Huang; Zefeng Zhang; Ju-Wei Yue; Jiawei Sheng; Quan-Gang Li; Chuang Zhang; Tingwen Liu

record.tranche_reason: Measures refusal-direction-projected attention-head scores under jailbreak prompts and reports how they change; this is a different, indirect measure of V3 than directly measuring or ablating the residual-stream direction.
record.gate_note: The paper uses a refusal direction to rank attention heads, but does not directly remove or add the direction. Its head-ablation results are not direction ablations. Table 1 reports AHD-versus-baseline attack outcomes, but AHD is the paper's own training method rather than an intervention on the claimed direction; Table 2 utility and Table 3 over-refusal results likewise do not test a listed version. Values used to select heads are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study computes the Arditi et al. difference-in-means refusal direction and projects attention-head outputs onto it. It reports that jailbreak prompts (SI-GCG, AutoDAN-GA/HGA, Adaptive) give lower cumulative projection than the original harmful prompt in four models. That is an indirect, component-level measure of whether attacks suppress the direction (V3). No direction ablation or addition is done (V1), and AHD trains with random head dropout, not against direction ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude safety behavior is concentrated in few, mostly middle-to-upper-layer attention heads, and that jailbreaks bypass or suppress them. They report that AHD spreads safety across heads, sharply lowers jailbreak harmfulness, and keeps utility without added over-refusal.
record.recipe_differences: The original work directly manipulates a difference-in-means residual-stream direction. This study uses that direction to score attention-head outputs, then masks heads; its AHD training drops heads rather than ablating the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The projected head-influence pattern varies by attack and head; in the Adaptive example, one head's score rises while the cumulative top-8 score falls. Ablation count also changes Qwen's rate of ambiguous responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking attention heads ranked by refusal-direction projection raises Llama-Guard harmfulness rates. Qwen increasingly gives ambiguous responses at high ablation counts (36% at 150 heads, 46% at 200).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention heads whose outputs align with the refusal direction are causally necessary for refusal; masking them impairs safety.

fits_no_version.finding: After AHD fine-tuning, harmfulness rises more gradually under head ablation in all four models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head-level dropout during safety fine-tuning distributes refusal-relevant computation across more heads.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The direct direction intervention in the claim is not performed. RDSHA uses 50 harmful prompts for its ablation evaluation, and the head-ablation plots give no numerical values in the text. Llama-Guard-3-8B is the automated harmfulness judge. The authors note that high ablation counts can yield short or incoherent outputs, and that Qwen ambiguity may not represent genuine safety. The paper also says its attack protocols differ and their harmfulness rates are not directly comparable.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. AHD-versus-baseline attack-rate results, utility benchmarks, and benign over-refusal rates were not extracted because they evaluate the paper's new training method rather than an intervention on the claimed refusal direction.

untested.parts: Whether jailbreaks suppress the residual-stream direction itself, as opposed to projections of individual head outputs. Whether training against direction ablation adds robustness: AHD drops random heads, not the direction. No statistics across prompts; one prompt per model.
No direction ablation or addition, and no capability check of a direction intervention. Head masking by projection rank is not direction ablation.
Not tested. Directions are recomputed separately for each model and each AHD variant.
Not tested. AHD changes how safety is distributed over heads, but direction existence or removability is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The V3 evidence is thin. It comes from one example prompt per model, figure-only, using an absolute-value projection of per-head outputs, with the top-8 heads presumably selected on the original prompt. The direction is derived with Arditi et al.'s official code, and its data may overlap the AdvBench evaluation prompts, which the authors argue does not matter. Table 1 AHD-versus-baseline attack rates are correctly left out: AHD is not training against direction ablation.

versions.untested_parts: No direct ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction, and no test of its effect on general capabilities.
Measures changes in projected attention-head influence scores under attacks, not direct suppression of the residual-stream direction or the effect of training against its ablation.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test.
AHD training changes head dropout during fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.

relation.reason: Section 3.4 and Appendix B.5 report the study's own measurement: under four jailbreak attacks in four models, head outputs project less onto the Arditi refusal direction. This bears on V3's 'attacks suppress this direction'.

tranche.reason: The recorded recipe compares the study with Arditi et al.'s ablation (V1). For V3, the original's own test was a suffix analysis. It projected the top eight heads' outputs onto the refusal direction under harmful vs. adversarial-suffix prompts. This rests on the original paper, not on files read here. Section 3.4 repeats that measure (top-8 heads, head output on the Arditi direction, original vs. jailbreak) with an absolute-valued summed score, new models and new attacks. That is arguably T1.

source_check.notes: AHD randomly drops heads during safety fine-tuning; it is not training against refusal-direction ablation, so Table 1 does not test V3's second clause. The figure values are lost in the text, and the Fig. 8–10 prompts were matched to models through the head-layer indices.

statements.correction: Text: arXiv v1, cs.CR, 27 Aug 2025; no venue stated. Projection result: one prompt per model, figure only, no control, no uncertainty. Score is the sum of |O_h·r|/||r|| over the top-8 heads. ± values (Tables 1–2), utility (Table 2) and over-refusal (Table 3) concern AHD fine-tuning, not the projection result.
statements.problem: The 'what' part is right. The 'why' part claims ICASSP review, controls and uncertainty. The text names no venue. The cited projection evidence has no control and no error bars. The ± values and the utility check apply only to the AHD results.

statements.correction: Llama2-7B-Chat, one prompt, Adaptive attack: H16.15's |O·r|/||r|| rises; H12.1 is almost completely bypassed; the top-8 cumulative score falls. The sign of H16.15's change is not shown.
statements.problem: The facts are right, but the evidence does not support reading them as a limit on V3. s_h is an absolute value, so H16.15's rise may be a larger negative projection. The top-8 sum still falls, and there is one prompt and one model.
Accurate as the study reports it. Caveat: the score is absolute-valued, and the top-8 sum still falls under the same attack.
